newsitem.title: UK: UK's Brown promises stable, dynamic economy.
newsitem.headline: UK's Brown promises stable, dynamic economy.

text.p: Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown on Tuesday promised British business leaders a stable economy and a new dynamism in industry.
To that end, he told the Confederation of British Industry's annual dinner, he would set up a new "enterprise and growth unit" within the Treasury to boost industrial innovation and entrepreneurship.

"We will identify the barriers to growth and productivity and then we will relentlessly work to remove them," Brown said, adding that Geoffrey Robinson, millionaire businessman and now Paymaster General, will head the unit.

"Stability is necessary for our future economic success," Brown said. "But stability for the long-term needs to be matched, in my view, by a new drive for dynamism and adaptability in industry, and by a new approach from government to wealth creation, employment and welfare."
Where there was a lack of research, a shortage of available technology, or if what is needed is help for exporters and small businesses -- "we want to help now," Brown said.
He repeated his assertion that Labour was committed to the long term. It would preside over no uncontrolled dashes for growth, no spiralling booms, no risk-taking with inflation.
He offered up his reforms to the monetary policy process, giving the Bank of England freedom to set interest rates, as proof of his commitment.

"Long-term interest rates fell after my announcment and I hope that the immediate welcome from the City and from industry will be matched by a recognition, over the long-term, of what we have done," Brown told the assembled captains of industry.

Another example of the new Labour administration's openness was provided by its invitation to the National Audit Office to comment on current forecasts for the public finances, Brown said. "No British Chancellor has ever done that before. I believe not only in sound public finance but in honesty and openness in public finance."

He said his forthcoming budget, due within weeks, would address the long-term needs of the British economy, setting tough rules for borrowing and spending in order to cut national debt over the medium-term.

Meanwhile, the government taskforce on taxes and benefits, unveiled on Monday and to be headed by Barclays chief executive Martin Taylor, would streamline and modernise the welfare state. "It will help achieve the government's objectives of encouraging hard work, reducing poverty and dependency and strengthening community and family life," Brown said.
Britain's new Chancellor also pledged a constructive approach to Europe, music to the ears of businessmen in a country where 60 percent of all trade is with the European Union.

"Let me put the government's position on Europe beyond doubt," he said. "We are in for the long-term, we are here to stay. And it is in Britain's essential interests that we now play a leading role in shaping Europe's future." Suspicion and distrust of Europe had suppressed sensible debate about a single European currency, Brown said, but he praised the CBI's attempts to keep the argument rooted in economic reality.

"British decisions on Europe and EMU need to be taken on the basis of intelligent, well-informed debate among all our people on what EMU will mean for British national interests in terms of jobs, investment and growth," he said.
